A-21 ACCESS AND AFFORDABILITY The University has developed a comprehensive enrollment management approach to foster access and affordability while also enhancing selectivity, quality, and student success.

Because of the University’s mission, the admissions policy is "selective" in that only students deemed prepared for university-level study are granted regular admission.

Feedback from families that choose URI is that the University offers quality programs in a safe location at a good cost and value.

Students admitted to TD have taken the required core academic courses in high school.
However, the average academic profile for students accepted to the TD program is not the average academic profile for students accepted through the regular admission process.
TD requires an intensive summer academic program prior to the start of the fall semester.
During the TD Summer Program students take university courses and live on campus.

TD students who successfully complete the TD Summer Program continue their enrollment at URI in the fall.
TD students receive academic and individual support from TD Advisors and mentors, and most receive the need based Hardge/Forleo Grant.
To be considered for the TD Program, students apply for admission to URI indicating their interest in TD, and then are considered through a competitive review process.

The Dean of Students is responsible for leading the university -wide Behavior Intervention Team and the Assistant Director of Outreach and Intervention leads the Students of Concern Team.
Staff frequently provide training to faculty and are available for consultation.

Talent Development.
Talent Development recruits and serves Rhode Island high school graduates with college potential who come from historically disadvantaged backgrounds .
Talent Development enrolls approximately 1,100 students annually and its mission is grounded in the University’s mission of enriching students' lives through its land, sea and urban grant traditions. (See “Talent Development” under “Access and Affordability”).
INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY SERVICES The University’s Information Technology Services organization (“ITS”) provides leadership, governance, and strategic direction for the technology and enterprise systems that support the University of Rhode Island community.
ITS is responsible for the relia bility, security, and ongoing modernization of systems that support instruction, research, administration, and daily University operations.
ITS supports core institutional systems used across the University, including the Learning Management System for online and in-person instruction; enterprise administrative systems supporting student records, human resources, and financial operations; and centralized support services through the University Help Desk.

ITS also operates and maintains the University’s high-speed network infrastructure, which connects URI campuses to one another and to national and global research networks through secure, multi -gigabit fiber-optic connectivity.
During the past year, the University expanded its research computing and artificial intelligence capabilities through the launch of the Institute for AI and Computational Research.
The Institute coordinates advanced computing, artificial intelligence, and data-intensive research activities across the University and strengthens URI’s participation at the Massachusetts Green High Performance Computing Center (MGHPCC), increasing available computing capacity, resilience, and access to shared regional infrastructure.
ITS provides artificial intelligence and research computing infrastructure not only for URI, but for nearly all public and private institutions of higher education in Rhode Island, excluding Brown University.
These services support the University of Rhode Island, Rhode Island College, Community College of Rhode Island, Bryant University, Salve Regina University, and other partner institutions.

This shared infrastructure model supports instruction, faculty research, and workforce development across the state and is provided to partner institutions at no cost.
To support the expanding use of artificial intelligence in teaching, research, and administrative functions, ITS launched a University -hosted AI platform based on LibreChat, deployed within a secure cloud environment.
The platform provides controlled acces s to multiple large language models hosted through

A-26 approved cloud providers and is designed to protect institutional and research data by isolating usage from public systems.
ITS has also deployed a secure version of Microsoft Copilot for all University faculty and staff, enabling productivity gains while maintaining institutional security and data governance standards.
Federal research sponsors increasingly require higher levels of data protection and compliance.
In response, ITS partnered with Hermathena Labs to provide secure research computing environments compliant with National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication 800-171 and Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification requirements.
In parallel, the University is developing its own higher-security research enclave, known as Sanctuary, at MGHPCC.
Sanctuary is intended to provide a University -controlled environment for sensitive, regulated, and export -controlled research workloads, expanding long -term institutional capacity and reducing reliance on third-party platforms as resources permit.
Cybersecurity remains a significant and evolving challenge for higher education.

ITS has continued to strengthen the University’s security posture through expanded use of multi-factor authentication, enhanced network monitoring and intrusion prevention cap abilities, and continued investment in disaster recovery and ransomware resilience.
These efforts are designed to reduce operational risk, protect sensitive information, and ensure continuity of academic and administrative services.
Despite these advances, ITS faces ongoing constraints related to staffing levels.
These constraints limit the pace at which new services can be expanded, legacy systems modernized, and emerging risks addressed.
As a result, certain enhancements in areas su ch as advanced security operations, expanded user support, and broader adoption of emerging technologies may require phased implementation over multiple years.
Through targeted investments and strategic partnerships, ITS supports student learning, faculty research, and institutional operations while managing risk and aligning technology capabilities with available resources and long-term University priorities.

FACILITIES The University’s current physical plant of 5. 7 million square feet across four campuses consists of 3 22 buildings (including leased buildings) including 24 residence halls, plus three apartment complexes and two dining centers, as well as the Memorial Union’s Ram’s Den.
Throughout its nearly continuous building program, the University has been successful in obtaining public financial support through the approval of bonds of the State issued for the benefit of the University for both renovation of older buildings and the construction of new buildings.
Over the last ten years, the University has completed more than $550 million in new construction and renovation and rehabilitation of existing structures.
Recent Completed Construction and Major Renovations: 2013 to 2024 Robert J.
Higgins Welcome Center.
September 26, 2018 marked the official opening of the $8.2 million Robert J.
Higgins Welcome Center, funded by generous donors and one -time University funding sources.

Located on a prominent site on Upper College Road, this new state of the art building is an important tool for continuing the growth in applications which has enabled the University to increase enrollment significantly over the last ten years in the face of declining numbers of high school graduates nationally and regionally, while simultaneo usly increasing both the quality of the student body and its diversity.
The Higgins Welcome Center showcases URI students and their successes and enhances that all-important first impression for prospective students and families upon arrival at the Kingston Campus.
The Fascitelli Center for Advanced Engineering (College of Engineering Phase I).
On October 7, 2019, the University dedicated The Fascitelli Center for Advanced Engineering, a new 187,000 square foot

A-27 building.
The phase 1 project started with the removal of five buildings that were built in the 1950s and 1960s to clear the site for the construction of the new building as well as renovation of the Kirk building.
The Fascitelli Center, funded by a generous donor as well as general obligation bonds issued by the State, comprises an east and west wing that are connected via what is effectively a truss bridge.
This center bridge manifests its structural members on the façade of the building, giving visual form to the engineering knowledge taught within which is in high demand by major employers in Rhode Island and serves as a draw to the State.

Meade Stadium Artificial Turf .

In 2019, the University of Rhode Island Athletic Department in conjunction with the Division of Student Affairs successfully completed the installation of an artificial surface and lights on Meade Stadium.
This project turned a facility that was used only six to eight times a year into one that can be used daily by URI’s varsity football program, along with general student use through intramurals and club sports.
This $4.1 million project, funded through $3 million of generous donor support and one-time Auxiliary Funding, was completed in time for the opening home football game on September 7, 2019.
Brookside Residence Hall.
The Brookside Residence Hall, an apartment-style residence hall on the west bank of the White Horn Brook on the Kingston campus, was dedicated on February 10, 2020.
This project is part of the University’s continuing initiative to provide safe, convenient, and affordable housing on the Kingston campus.
This state-of-the-art residence facility provides 500 new beds in an apartment-style six- story building focusing on upperclassmen.

In addition to providing safe and affordable housin g, working with the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management, this project restored the section of White Horn Brook from Flagg Road to West Alumni Avenue, providing wildlife habitat, campus amenities, and stormwater improvements for this area of campus.
As an added amenity to the students living in Brookside and others on campus, this project provided the final northern connection to the campus bike path.
This bike path is now complete from Flagg Road heading south for approximately two miles to connect with the eight-mile William C.
O'Neill Bike Path that leads from the historic Kingston train station to the beaches in Narragansett.
Ranger Hall Phase II.
The Ranger Hall Phase II renovation was completed in August 2022.
This project built on the success of phase one, which opened in the fall of 2016 with the expansion of the Harrington School of Communication and Media to the second, third, and fourth floors of this historic building on the Kingston campus.

This renovation of the upper floors of Ranger Hall, funded by a generous private gift, provides the Harrington School with high technology classroom space to advance the Harrington School of Communication and Media as well as much needed general assignment classrooms in the heart of the academic core of the campus.
Soloviev Basketball Practice Facility.
In the fall of 2023, the University completed an $8.0 million privately fundraised renovation of the Soloviev Basketball Practice Facility.
This facility provides 24-hour access to state -of-the-art training facilities for URI’s highly competitive men's an d women's basketball programs.
Infrastructure.
In the 2018 legislative session $19.8 million of much needed paving ($11 million), infrastructure ($6.5 million) and auxiliary fire protection ($2.3 million) projects were approved for revenue bond financing.
Working with RIHEBC these bonds have been issued in support of further improvements

A-28 of the campus’ hardscape, infrastructure and life safety needs.

Phase Three of the University's progressive efforts to repave and reconstruct major parking facilities, internal roadways, walkways, and drainage systems across three of its four campuses has been completed.
The University has upgraded the high voltage electrical substations and electrical infrastructure on the Kingston Campus.
Work was completed on a new substation at Butterfield Road and an expanded substation on Flagg Road.
Improvements were made to the existing electrical system to support flexible back -feed capability throughout the system.

Projects in Progress Narragansett Bay Campus Renewal – Phase I.
Leading an East Coast Oceanographic Consortium, the University of Rhode Island’s Graduate School of Oceanography in 2018 secured the management contract for a new, $125 million National Science Foundation (NSF) Regional Class Research Vessel, the Narraganset Dawn.
This vessel’s home base will be URI’s Narragansett Bay Campus.
To support this and other cutting-edge research that is ongoing at the Narragansett Bay Campus, in November 2018, Rhode Island voters approved $45 million of general obligation bonds of the State to support the project.
Phase IA of this project is the construction of a new, larger pier for the NSF research vessel.
The pier is substantially complete.Phase 1B of this project is to deliver the Ocean Robotics Laboratory, which will be completed in April 2026.
This building will bring together faculty from the Graduate School of Oceanography and the Ocean Engineering department.

Equipment and robotics pioneered here will work hand -in-glove with the new Regional Class Research Vessel, Narragansett Dawn, and its advanced overboard -handling systems for launch and recovery of scientific equipment at sea.
Moreover, the 33,000 square-foot facility will create opportunities for collaborations within URI, among university partners and through public-private ventures.
Narragansett Bay Campus Renewal – Phase II.
In November 2022, Rhode Island voters approved the issuance of $100 million in State of Rhode Island general obligation bonds to support the second phase of the renewal of the Narragansett Bay Campus including the replacement of the antiquated buildings housing the Graduate School of Oceanography (“GSO”) and Ocean Engineering (“OE”).

The replacement of the Ocean Engineering Complex will provide the ability for OE to continue to lead the State forward in the development of Rhode Island’s Blue Economy as URI continues to lead these efforts toward economic growth in this important sector.

In the 2020 session the legislature approved the referendum for $57.3 million in general obligation bonds to go before State voters to recapitalize the Fine Arts Center.
State voters generously approved the bond as part of a special election in March 2021.
This project will remove two antiquated building pods from the complex renovate three building pods and construct a new three - story building to provide new space for the Art, Theater and Music departments.
Construction on the Fine Arts Center is underway and will complete in the Spring of 2026.
Water Filtration Plant.
At the end of the Fiscal Year 2022 legislative session, the Rhode Island General Assembly enacted legislation that establishes a concentration limit of 20 parts per trillion of Per - and Polyfluorinated Substances (“PFAS”) in public drinking water supplies.
The legislation established the Rhode Island Department of Health as the regulatory body for monitoring compliance with this new

A-29 standard.
The Environmental Protection Agency in March 2023 has similarly proposed to establish legally enforceable levels for six PFAS known to occur in drinking water, and this proposed rule is currently out for comment.
The University, which is licensed as a municipal -level water system subject to the newly enacted Rhode Island law, received $20 million in RICAP funds support from the state of Rhode Island to design and construct a water system filtration plant.
As of November 2024, the first phase of construction of the filtration plant was completed with that phase 1 effort successfully supplying “PFAS-free” water to the campus.
Next steps include completing design efforts for Phase 2 of the filtration plant that expands the plants capabilities and extends the useful life of the plant for the next 20-30 years.
The university anticipates awarding a design -build-operate contract in 2026, with intended phase 2 completion by fiscal year -end 2027.

RICAP funds are “pay -as-you-go” State surplus funds dedicated to capital maintenance which enable the State to reduce the amount of debt – and thus expense - incurred for this purpose.

ENTERPRISE RISK MANAGEMENT The University has instituted an Enterprise Risk Management (“ERM”) program.
ERM is the formal and systematic effort to control the impact of uncertainty and variability on an organization’s strategic objectives by managing risks at all levels of the organization.
ERM differs from traditional risk management by taking a holistic approach to managing risk.
As part of the ERM program, the University procures appropriate insurance as one of many risk control and mitigation measures.
The University is insured for various risks of loss arising out of claims for negligence, including bodily injury and property damage, wrongful acts, cyber liability, professional liability and workers compensation through a combination of insurance polici es and self -insurance.

The University’s property insurance program covers University buildings and contents against risks of dire ct physical loss, on a blanket, replacement cost basis.
As of Jan 2026, total property value for the University’s four campuses is reported as $2.3 billion.
There is a $250,000 deductible per building for damage caused by a Named Windstorm and a $200,000 deductible for any other peril on an aggregated basis.
Total property coverage is $240,000,000.

Parlange, Ph.D., P.Eng., President DATE: February 2, 2026 SUBJECT: Action Item: Consideration of a Resolution on Bond Reimbursement Purpose of Submittal: The University is seeking approval from the Board of Trustees for a resolution allowing for the reimbursement of expenditures related to two infrastructure projects that may be made by the University prior to the issuance of debt supporting these projects.
The University anticipates seeking authorization from the Board to issue a revenue bond in fall 2026 to support both projects.
The proposed reimbursement amount would be capped at $6.91M, which equals the portion of the project costs anticipated to be spent between now and bond issuance, with a 15% contingency buffer.

The two projects are: 1) Utility Infrastructure Upgrade – Phase III (total project cost: $9.1M) 2) Repaving and Hardscape Improvements (total project cost: $20M) Points to Consider: URI has a history of funding capital expenditures through the issuance of tax-exempt bonds, repayment of which is made over a period of years that does not exceed the useful life of the capital assets being financed.
These tax- exempt bonds are subject to federal regulations that, among other matters, limit arbitrage or require rebate of earnings in certain circumstances and require ongoing compliance.
Federal tax regulations provide that the University can advance its own funds to pay capital expenditures prior to the issuance of tax-exempt bonds, use such bond proceeds to reimburse itself for the advanced funds, and treat such bond proceeds as being “spent” for federal tax purposes when the reimbursement is made, thus avoiding further tax compliance with respect to such funds.

To avail itself of the ability to make such reimbursement, under the applicable tax regulations, the University must declare its “official intent” prior to making the capital expenditures expected to be reimbursed from bond proceeds.
URI is seeking this declaration of “official intent” from the Board to reimburse itself for funds related to two projects currently on the University’s Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) that will be debt-financed through revenue bonds contemplated to be issued in Fall 2026, pending Board of Trustees approval.
These two projects would begin in summer 2026.
URI has already received Kushner authorization to issue th e Utility Infrastructure Phase III project bond, and the Kushner for the Parking and Repaving project is included in the FY27 Governor’s request and is currently under review by the General Assembly.

The projected expenditures proposed for reimbursement for the Utility Infrastructure Phase III project is $4.51M, to replace the Farmhouse Road Steam line. The projected expenditures for the Parking and Hardscape project, to replace parking lost by the construction of a new residence hall, is $1.5M. The total amount of projected reimbursement is $6.01M. Recommendation: I recommend that the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees approve the resolution to allow for the reimbursement of certain expenditures made prior to the issuance of the bond funding the projects noted here.
